assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative-data evidence transformed the empirical study of intergenerational mobility and its geographic and institutional correlates.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren and Friedman are central to the linked-data measurement and research programme; credit beyond three people remains a constraint.
assessment.maturity: The findings are extensively used in research and public-policy discussion, with a substantial accumulated body of evidence.
uncertainties: The appropriate division between measurement, causal interpretation and broader collaborative contributions remains contestable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work made technology, tasks and trade shocks central empirical mechanisms for understanding changing labour demand and wage inequality.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson provide a coherent core for the task and China-shock evidence, though related contributions are broad.
assessment.maturity: The research has had durable influence across labour, trade and policy debates.
uncertainties: Quantitative estimates and their interpretation continue to be debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Audit and correspondence designs supplied unusually direct and influential evidence on discrimination in labour markets.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan are especially closely associated with the landmark correspondence-study contribution; Charles represents the broader discrimination research programme.
assessment.maturity: The approach has been replicated and adapted widely, making its empirical contribution mature.
uncertainties: Audit-study estimates may not map fully to all margins of discrimination or all labour markets.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The programme established that early-life health and environments have persistent economic consequences and sharpened the study of skill formation.
assessment.attribution: Currie, Almond and Cunha make complementary empirical and conceptual contributions, although the literature has many important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Long-run evidence and subsequent work across countries give the area considerable maturity.
uncertainties: Causal channels and the portability of particular early-life interventions remain uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Research on employer market power revised a fundamental benchmark for labour-market analysis and has important policy implications.
assessment.attribution: Manning is the clearest foundational figure; Ashenfelter and Naidu represent major empirical and modern contributions.
assessment.maturity: The framework has become highly influential and is supported by a growing empirical literature.
uncertainties: The magnitude and sources of monopsony vary substantially across settings.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Elasticity-of-taxable-income research created a practical empirical basis for evaluating behavioural responses and optimal income taxation.
assessment.attribution: Saez and Slemrod are central to the tax-response and public-finance programme; Chetty contributed important identification and behavioural work.
assessment.maturity: The methods and estimates have deeply influenced tax research and policy analysis over many years.
uncertainties: Reported elasticities depend on tax institutions, avoidance opportunities and identification choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The research reshaped analysis of teacher quality, school incentives and educational production using increasingly credible empirical designs.
assessment.attribution: Kane, Hanushek and Hoxby are leading contributors, though the candidate grouping combines several partially distinct literatures.
assessment.maturity: The evidence has accumulated over decades and strongly affected education-policy debate.
uncertainties: Accountability and teacher-policy effects are context dependent, and attribution to a three-person award is difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theory and measurement of adverse selection substantially improved understanding of insurance-market failures and policy design.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein, Einav and Salanie form a credible theory-and-evidence grouping, though foundational work extends beyond them.
assessment.maturity: The framework has been tested in multiple insurance settings and is well integrated into applied microeconomics.
uncertainties: Selection, moral hazard and market institutions can be difficult to separate empirically.
